```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(rblat)
# Paths to the vendored trellis regression fixtures (see
# inst/extdata/trellis/README.md for provenance).
ex <- function(...) system.file("extdata", "trellis", ..., package = "rblat")
```

## Motivation: the `trellis` re-alignment step

`trellis` detects somatic structural rearrangements from whole-genome sequencing.
A key quality-control step re-aligns candidate reads with
[BLAT](https://genome.ucsc.edu/FAQ/FAQblat.html): reads that were unmapped (or
suspiciously mapped) near a candidate junction are re-aligned to check whether
they support a *novel* sequence junction rather than mapping cleanly elsewhere.

Today that step shells out to the command-line `blat` binary. Concretely,
`trellis` does something like:

```{r trellis-today, eval = FALSE}
## --- how trellis re-aligns reads today (illustrative) ---
## `tags` is a data.frame of reads with columns qname, read, seq, ...
writeToFasta(tags, "reads.fa")                       # write a query FASTA
cmd <- paste("blat", "-minScore=0", "-stepSize=1",   # shell out to the binary
             "reference.fa", "reads.fa", "out.psl")
system(cmd)                                          # external process
blat <- readBlat("out.psl")                          # read the .psl back in
blat <- annotateBlatRecords(blat, tags)              # downstream QC
rear <- blatScores(blat, tags, id = "SAMPLE")        # pass/fail per rearrangement
```

That works, but it carries the usual costs of an external binary: `blat` must be
installed and on the `PATH`, the pipeline pays process-spawn and disk-I/O
overhead for every sample, and the FASTA/PSL temp files are a source of
portability and reproducibility friction.

**`rblat` runs the very same BLAT engine inside R via `.Call`** — no `system()`
call, no external binary, and (optionally) no files at all. The result is the
identical 21-column PSL `data.frame` that `readBlat()` produces, so it drops
straight into the existing downstream code.

```{r version}
rblat_version()
```

## Step 1 — a drop-in for the command-line call

The most conservative change keeps FASTA files exactly where they are and only
replaces the `system("blat …")` + `readBlat()` pair with a single `rblat()`
call. `rblat()` accepts FASTA paths for both the target/database and the query:

```{r file-mode}
# These fixtures are the exact inputs from trellis/svbams's blat test, bundled
# with rblat. `golden.psl` is the output of the *external* command-line blat.
aln <- rblat(ex("ref1.fa"), ex("query1.fa"),
             minScore = 0, stepSize = 1)   # same flags trellis passes
aln[, c("match", "strand", "Qname", "Tname", "Tstart", "Tend",
        "blockcount", "blockSizes")]
```

The column names are exactly `trellis`'s `blat_colnames`, in the same order:

```{r colnames}
identical(names(aln), blat_colnames)
```

And the result is **byte-for-byte identical** to what the external command-line
`blat` produced on the same inputs — `rblat` ships those real command-line
goldens so this equivalence is checked on every build:

```{r golden}
golden <- readPsl(ex("golden1.psl"))   # output of external command-line blat
identical(aln, golden)
```

So a first-pass integration is a one-line swap:

```{r swap, eval = FALSE}
## before:
writeToFasta(tags, "reads.fa"); system(paste("blat …", "reads.fa", "out.psl"))
blat <- readBlat("out.psl")
## after:
blat <- rblat("reference.fa", "reads.fa", minScore = 0, stepSize = 1)
```

Everything downstream (`annotateBlatRecords()`, `blatScores()`, …) is unchanged
because it receives the identical `data.frame`.

## Step 2 — a more direct integration (no files)

The re-alignment reads already live in memory as a `data.frame` — `trellis`
*writes* them to a FASTA only because the external `blat` needs a file. `rblat`
removes that constraint: pass the sequences directly as a **named character
vector** (names are the sequence identifiers) or a `Biostrings::DNAStringSet`.
The whole alignment then touches no disk at all.

```{r mem-mode}
# A named character vector: names = identifiers, values = sequences.
# (Here we read the fixtures in, but in trellis these come straight from `tags`.)
read_fasta <- function(path) {
  ln <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE); ln <- ln[nzchar(ln)]
  h  <- grepl("^>", ln)
  nm <- sub("[[:space:]].*$", "", sub("^>", "", ln[h]))
  sq <- tapply(gsub("[[:space:]]", "", ln[!h]), cumsum(h)[!h], paste, collapse = "")
  stats::setNames(as.character(sq), nm)
}
ref   <- read_fasta(ex("ref1.fa"))
reads <- read_fasta(ex("query1.fa"))
str(reads)

aln_mem <- rblat(ref, reads, minScore = 0, stepSize = 1)
identical(aln_mem, golden)   # same answer as the file-based / command-line run
```

`Biostrings` sequences work the same way, which is convenient when the reads are
already carried as an `XStringSet`:

```{r biostrings, eval = requireNamespace("Biostrings", quietly = TRUE)}
ref_ss   <- Biostrings::DNAStringSet(ref)
reads_ss <- Biostrings::DNAStringSet(reads)
identical(rblat(ref_ss, reads_ss, minScore = 0, stepSize = 1), golden)
```

## What a future `trellis` integration could look like

Because `trellis` already holds the reads as a `data.frame` (`tags`, with
`qname`, `read`, and `seq` columns), the direct integration collapses the
write-FASTA / spawn-blat / read-PSL trio into a single in-memory call. A thin
adapter — living in `trellis`, not requiring any change to `rblat` — might be:

```{r future, eval = FALSE}
## Candidate replacement for the external-blat step, no files, no system():
realignReads <- function(tags, reference, ...) {
  # trellis already names reads "qname_read" when writing the FASTA
  reads <- setNames(tags$seq, paste(tags$qname, tags$read, sep = "_"))
  reads <- reads[!duplicated(names(reads))]
  rblat(reference, reads, minScore = 0, stepSize = 1, ...)   # -> blat_colnames df
}

blat <- realignReads(tags, reference = "reference.fa")
blat <- annotateBlatRecords(blat, tags)     # unchanged
rear <- blatScores(blat, tags, id = "SAMPLE")
```

`reference` can itself be in-memory (a `DNAStringSet` of the local windows around
each candidate junction), so a per-junction re-alignment need not read or write
a single file. The return value is the same `blat_colnames` `data.frame`
`readBlat()` returns, so `annotateBlatRecords()` and `blatScores()` are
untouched. This keeps `rblat` a self-contained provider that `trellis` can adopt
incrementally: swap the `system()` call first (Step 1), then drop the FASTA
round-trip when convenient (Step 2).

> **Note.** This vignette illustrates the integration; it does not modify
> `trellis`. `rblat`'s own test suite regression-tests these fixtures against the
> command-line-blat goldens shown above, so the equivalence downstream code
> relies on is verified without any dependency on `trellis`.

## Options and modes

`rblat()` exposes BLAT's common tuning options as named arguments. Each numeric
option defaults to `NULL`, meaning "use BLAT's own *type-aware* default" (e.g.
`tileSize` is 11 for DNA but 5 for protein); set a value only to override.

```{r options, eval = FALSE}
rblat(ref, reads, minScore = 30, minIdentity = 95)   # stricter DNA search
rblat(ref, reads, t = "prot", q = "prot")            # protein vs protein
rblat(ref, reads, oneOff = TRUE, fastMap = TRUE)      # logical flags
rblat(ref, reads, args = c("-fine"))                  # raw pass-through flags
```

A query with no acceptable alignment returns a well-typed **empty**
`data.frame` (not an error), so downstream `nrow()`/`rbind()` logic is safe:

```{r empty}
empty <- rblat(ref, reads, minScore = 10000)   # impossibly high threshold
nrow(empty)
identical(names(empty), blat_colnames)
```
